claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: Like other aspects of TypeScript’s type system, private and protected are only enforced during type checking. | private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking. [probe-01: exit 0]
claim_checks.note: The handbook supports the type-check-only enforcement and runtime access for both modifiers. It allows bracket access during type checking, and calls the field 'soft private', for `private` only. The `protected` bracket-access part rests on probe-01 alone. The probe is valid: tsc would exit non-zero if the access were rejected. But it shows only what TypeScript 5.9.3 did, and the claim states it as a general rule with no version.

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks will degrade performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. | Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: The page says 'could affect' and the claim says 'will degrade'. 'Will' is a MUST-level word, so this raises the modal. The claim also applies the note to the downlevelled WeakMaps only. The page's note covers every hard runtime privacy mechanism: closures, WeakMaps and private fields.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` copies them like public fields.
claim_checks.page_says: structuredClone() does not clone private elements | they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method. [probe-02 stdout: false]
claim_checks.note: The first sentence is entailed. The structuredClone part says the opposite of MDN. The doc's own probe-02 is valid, because it would print true if the field were copied, and in Node 24.22.1 it prints false: the clone has no #x. The doc's Probes section says the same, so the doc contradicts itself. No cited source supports the claim, so this is a misreading, counted once here as a grounding finding and not as a separate KB-17 source conflict.

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: If you access a private element from an object that doesn't have the element, a TypeError is thrown | return true if the private field or method exists, and false otherwise
claim_checks.note: The page's example error text reads 'from an object whose class did not declare it'.

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.4 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: The first issue has been fixed in V8 v9.7 | Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call for class field initializations.
claim_checks.note: The page gives v9.7 and the claim gives 9.4, a different version number. The doc's own front matter says 'V8 ≥ 9.7'.

claim_checks.claim: A `#` name cannot be a parameter property (row: An injected collaborator (port, clock, logger) | `private readonly x` constructor parameter)
claim_checks.page_says: Allow `#`-private names in parameter property positions | That this is not possible is a bit surprising
claim_checks.note: The text supports the claim, but the source is Rank 6 (an issue tracker) and is cited in a role 3 section. That KB-15 breach is a CRITICAL_FAIL, listed under violations.

claim_checks.claim: Object wrapped in a `Proxy` (some mocking and reactivity libraries) | `#` access does not go through the proxy | Private elements cannot be proxied
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.

claim_checks.claim: Target ES2021 or lower | `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups | TypeScript downlevels it
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: Working around it with `--experimental-transform-types` | Runs on Node 24.22 with an `ExperimentalWarning` (re-tested 2026-11-03); the flag is removed in Node 26.0.0 | So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor
claim_checks.page_says: Removed --experimental-transform-types flag. [listed under v26.0.0]; not found: 'ExperimentalWarning', any 24.22 mention (searched 'experimental', 'v24.22')
claim_checks.note: The removal in v26.0.0 is entailed. The Node 24.22 behaviour, a run with an ExperimentalWarning, comes from a local re-test that no probe or cited page records. The saved page is the Node.js v26.13.1 documentation, so it does not cover the 24.22 runtime. The 'keep readonly #fields' advice is the doc's own inference.

claim_checks.claim: Type stripping itself | Stable (stability 2) since Node 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; Node ignores `tsconfig.json` and needs `.ts` extensions in relative imports | Node only deletes types
claim_checks.page_says: Type stripping is now stable. | Type stripping no longer emits an experimental warning. | Node.js ignores tsconfig.json files | file extensions are mandatory in import statements
claim_checks.note: Everything else is entailed (stable in v25.2.0 and v24.12.0, Stability: 2, tsconfig ignored, extensions mandatory, only inline types removed). But the page says only that the experimental warning stopped in v24.3.0 and v22.18.0. The claim drops 'experimental' and says 'no warning'.

claim_checks.claim: In Node 24.22.1, `Object.getOwnPropertyNames()` never lists a `#` field
claim_checks.note: The probe cannot fail. An empty `catch {}` swallows every error, and `console.log('not listed')` runs unconditionally after the try block. Its only check, `names.length > 5`, never looks for a # field. The output is the same whatever getOwnPropertyNames returns.

violations.evidence: C3: item 3 says the handbook notes runtime privacy checks 'will degrade performance'. [^1] says these checks 'could affect performance', so a 'could' becomes a 'will' (MUST level). The note is also narrowed from all hard runtime privacy mechanisms to the WeakMap downlevel.
C4: item 4 says structuredClone() copies private elements like public fields. [^2] says 'structuredClone() does not clone private elements', and the doc's own probe-02 printed false in Node 24.22.1.
C6: item 6 dates the inline-cache fast path for class-field initialization to V8 9.4. [^3] says it was fixed in V8 v9.7 ('Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call').
C12: probe-03 wraps its work in try { … } catch {} and prints 'not listed' unconditionally. It cannot fail, so it backs nothing (invalid_probe).

The 'Where each form fits' table row 'A # name cannot be a parameter property ✅[^5]' cites a Rank 6 source (a github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/ page) in a role 3 section, which allows ranks 1–4 only.

C1: [^1] gives bracket-notation access during type checking, and 'soft private', for `private` only. The claim extends both to `protected`. That part rests on probe-01 alone (TypeScript 5.9.3) but is worded as a general rule with no version.
C10: 'Runs on Node 24.22 with an ExperimentalWarning (re-tested 2026-11-03)' is not in [^4], which is the Node.js v26.13.1 documentation, and no probe records it.
C11: 'no warning since 24.3.0' drops a qualifier. [^4] says 'Type stripping no longer emits an experimental warning' (v24.3.0, v22.18.0).
[^6] (TC39 class fields proposal) is listed with 'Backs: How it works 2', but the body never cites [^6]: How it works item 2 cites only [^1].

The status line says 'Verified: 10 claims (✅)', but the body has 12 ✅-closed claims (14 ✅ marks). The Summary ('reading and creating # fields costs the same as public fields' on any native ES2022+ target) and the Takeaways ('measured cost is nil') generalize one Node 24.22 / V8 13.6 measurement. Neither is marked, and neither cites an artifact.

The doc has no role 2 (concept architecture) or role 5 (reference & invariants) section. The exact Node version history sits in the Edge cases table. 'How it works' mixes a design decision table ('Where each form fits') into the mechanism steps.

patch_instructions.action: Item 3: replace 'The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks will degrade performance.' with 'The handbook notes that hard runtime privacy mechanisms (closures, WeakMaps or private fields) could affect performance.' ✅[^1] ("Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.")

Item 4: replace 'and `structuredClone()` copies them like public fields' with 'and `structuredClone()` does not clone them; `Object.freeze()` and `Object.seal()` have no effect on them' ✅[^2]. Keep ✅[^probe-02] only as the Node 24.22.1 observation that the clone has no `#x`.
Item 6: change 'V8 9.4' to 'V8 v9.7' per [^3] ('The first issue has been fixed in V8 v9.7'; 'Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call for class field initializations').

Rewrite probe-03 so it can fail: drop the try/catch and print the actual names, e.g. `const names = Object.getOwnPropertyNames(new (class { #x = 1; y = 2 })()); console.log(JSON.stringify(names));` with expect="stdout:[\"y\"]". Reword the claim as 'In Node 24.22.1, Object.getOwnPropertyNames() on an instance with `#x` and `y` returns ["y"]'. Until it is re-run, mark the claim ⚠️. The general rule can instead cite [^2] ('cannot be … interacted with using any Object method').

'Where each form fits', row 3: drop ✅[^5] from the role 3 table. Either cite [^1] for what it does say ('parameter properties … are created by prefixing a constructor argument with one of the visibility modifiers public, private, protected, or readonly'), or move 'A # name cannot be a parameter property' into Edge cases or Trade-offs (role 6), citing [^5] marked as Rank 6.

Item 1: limit bracket-notation access during type checking and the 'soft private' label to `private` per [^1]. Add a separate observation: 'In TypeScript 5.9.3, bracket access to a `protected` member also type-checks ✅[^probe-01]'.

Row '--experimental-transform-types': keep 'removed in Node 26.0.0 ✅[^4]'. Mark the Node 24.22 ExperimentalWarning run ⚠️ as a local observation, or back it with a node24 probe that checks stderr for ExperimentalWarning.
Row 'Type stripping itself': change 'no warning since 24.3.0' to 'no experimental warning since 24.3.0 (and 22.18.0)' per [^4].
Cite [^6] where the References entry says it backs, e.g. append ✅[^6] to How it works item 2 (the proposal: 'Private fields provide a strong encapsulation boundary'), or remove the [^6] entry.
Recount the ✅ claims after the fixes. Qualify the Summary and Takeaways performance statements as 'measured on Node 24.22 (V8 13.6)' and point them to the Worked example, or mark them ⚠️.

Move the 'Where each form fits' decision table to Trade-offs. Consider a short Reference section (role 5) for the exact values: type-stripping version history, the WeakMap downlevel threshold (ES2021) and the V8 v9.7 fast path, each cited to a rank 1–4 source.
